analogy.p: Imagine a duvet thrown over a bed with a pile of books under one corner: the corner with the books (the north and west) is high and lumpy, because hard, resistant rock props it up, and the rest sinks down smoothly (the south and east), where there are only soft pillows underneath. Rain that lands on the lumps trickles down towards the flat side. This breaks down because a real landscape also has tilting, folding and glacial sculpting, not just a static pile.
analogy.t: The UK as a lumpy duvet

bullets: **Landscape** = the visible features of an area of land, including relief (height and shape), rock type, rivers, coast, vegetation and human use.
The UK's physical landscape is described using three key ideas: **relief** (height and steepness), **geology** (rock types and structure) and **drainage** (where the rivers flow).
The simplest summary is **highland Britain in the north and west, lowland Britain in the south and east**.
Landscapes are the result of long-term processes (tectonics, weathering, erosion, glaciation) acting on different rock types, then modified by people.
Exam questions usually ask you to **describe the distribution** of something on a map, or to **explain** why it is there; you need both skills.
Link to later topics: the coasts topic, the rivers topic and the glacial topic all use the same relief and rock-type ideas introduced here.
core.h: The big picture: a country of contrasts
core.p: The UK is small but has a remarkable variety of landscapes packed into a short distance. Within a few hundred kilometres you can travel from flat, low-lying farmland in East Anglia to steep glaciated mountains in the Scottish Highlands, and from soft crumbling cliffs in Holderness to hard rocky headlands in Cornwall. The spec asks for an **overview of the physical landscape of the UK**: where the **uplands** and **lowlands** are, where the main **rivers** run, and why the pattern looks the way it does. Everything you later learn about coasts, rivers and glaciation sits on top of this basic map.

bullets: **Altitude** is height above sea level, measured in metres (m).
**Contour lines** close together = a **steep** slope; contour lines far apart = a **gentle** slope; no lines = flat land.

An **upland** area is generally higher ground, often above about 200 m, and is usually rugged, steeper and cooler and wetter. A **lowland** area is lower, flatter, usually below about 200 m, and warmer and drier.
The term **mountain** is often used for land above about 600 m; hills are lower and gentler.
Describing relief: give height values from the key (e.g. rises from 50 m in the east to over 400 m in the west), mention steepness, and name the direction.
Relief affects human activity: steep, high, wet land suits sheep farming, forestry, water supply and tourism; flat, low land suits arable farming, large settlements and transport.
core.h: Relief: what it means and how it is shown
core.p: **Relief** describes the height and shape of the land surface. Geographers describe relief using words such as high, low, steep, gentle, flat, rugged and undulating. On maps it is shown using **contour lines** (lines joining points of equal height above sea level), **spot heights**, **layer colouring** (usually green for low, brown for high) and sometimes shading. Being able to read relief from a map is a core skill because it lets you identify upland and lowland areas and describe slopes.

bullets: **Scottish Highlands** (northern Scotland): the highest land in the UK, including **Ben Nevis** (1345 m, the UK's highest mountain).
**Southern Uplands** (southern Scotland, near the border): lower, rounder hills than the Highlands.
**Lake District / Cumbrian Mountains** (north-west England): includes **Scafell Pike** (978 m), the highest mountain in England; classic glaciated scenery.
**Pennines** (the 'backbone of England' running north to south through northern England): hills and moorland, source of many rivers.
**Snowdonia (Eryri)** in north Wales: includes **Snowdon** (1085 m), the highest mountain in Wales and England and Wales combined.
**Cambrian Mountains** (mid-Wales) and the **Brecon Beacons** (south Wales).
**Dartmoor and Exmoor** in south-west England: lower uplands, with Dartmoor made of granite (High Willhays about 621 m).
**Northern Ireland**: the **Mourne Mountains** (Slieve Donard about 850 m) and Antrim Plateau.
core.p: The main upland areas are found in the **north and west** of the UK. Many are made of old, hard rock that has resisted erosion, and most were shaped by glaciers during the last Ice Age, which left steep valleys, corries and sharp ridges. You need to be able to name and locate the major upland areas on an outline map and give an example of a high point in each.

bullets: **East Anglia** and **the Fens**: extremely flat, reclaimed wetland, in places close to or even below sea level; very fertile arable farmland.
**London Basin / Thames Valley**: low-lying clay basin surrounded by chalk hills (the Chilterns and North Downs).
**Cheshire Plain, Vale of York, Midlands plain and Somerset Levels**: flat or gently rolling lowlands in the middle and west of England.
**Central Lowlands of Scotland** (the Forth and Clyde valley): a rift valley where most Scots live.
**Chalk uplands in the south-east**: Chilterns, North and South Downs, Salisbury Plain are low hills (mostly under 300 m), showing that the south-east is not totally flat.
Lowlands have **gentle slopes**, deep soils, a mild drier climate, and good transport routes, so they hold most of the UK's cities and industry.
Remember that 'lowland' does not mean 'flat': the Weald and the Downs are lowland but have rolling hills.
core.p: Lowlands are mostly in the **south and east** of the UK. They are made largely of younger, softer sedimentary rocks such as clay, chalk and sand, which erode more easily and so form gentler, lower relief. Rivers in lowlands are slow flowing and meander, and deposition builds flat floodplains. These are the areas with the best farmland and the largest populations.

bullets: **Igneous rock**: formed when molten magma or lava cools and solidifies; very hard and resistant, e.g. **granite** (Dartmoor, Cornish coast, Scottish Highlands), basalt.

**Sedimentary rock**: formed from layers of sediment compressed and cemented over millions of years, often in layers (beds) with joints; e.g. **limestone**, **chalk**, **sandstone**, **clay** (clay is soft; chalk and limestone are porous and have joints).
**Metamorphic rock**: sedimentary or igneous rock changed by heat and pressure, e.g. **slate**, **marble**; generally hard and resistant.
**Resistant (hard) rock** erodes slowly and forms upland, cliffs and headlands; **less resistant (soft) rock** erodes quickly and forms lowland, bays and wide valleys.
**Permeable** rocks (chalk, limestone, sandstone) allow water to pass through; **impermeable** rocks (clay, granite) do not, causing surface water, springs and marshes.
The **Tees-Exe line** is a generalisation; there are soft rocks in the north-west (e.g. the Cheshire Plain) and hard rocks in the south-east, so use words like 'generally'.
Why does geology matter? Differences in rock type produce differences in landscape, soils, drainage, farming and settlement.
core.h: Geology: rock types and the Tees-Exe line
core.p: The pattern of highlands and lowlands is mainly explained by **geology**. An imaginary line from the mouth of the River Tees in the north-east to the mouth of the River Exe in the south-west (the **Tees-Exe line**) divides the UK roughly in two. North and west of the line the rocks are generally **older and harder** (igneous and metamorphic rocks such as granite and slate, plus hard sedimentary rocks like millstone grit and old limestones), forming high, rugged land. South and east of the line the rocks are generally **younger and softer** (clay, chalk, sands), forming lower, gentler land. This is the best single explanation to give in an exam.

bullets: Old mountain ranges (built when plates collided) have been eroded over hundreds of millions of years, leaving rounded hills in places (e.g. Southern Uplands) and hard rock cores.

During the **last glacial period**, ice sheets covered Scotland, northern England, Wales and Ireland; ice reached roughly as far south as the Bristol Channel and the Thames region at its maximum extent in earlier glaciations.
Glaciation produced **U-shaped valleys, corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks and ribbon lakes** in the highlands (e.g. Lake District, Snowdonia).
South of the ice limit, **periglacial conditions** (very cold, tundra-like) caused freeze-thaw weathering but no ice cover.
When the ice melted, sea levels rose, flooding valleys and shaping the modern coastline.

Prevailing south-westerly winds bring moist air from the Atlantic; the western uplands force it to rise, giving **relief rainfall** (over 2000 mm a year in the Lake District), which feeds many rivers.
**Link**: the glacial landscapes topic expands on these landforms.
core.h: Why highland Britain is in the north and west: tectonic and ice history
core.p: The older rocks of the north and west were formed or deformed hundreds of millions of years ago, during periods of mountain building (collisions of tectonic plates) that created huge ranges, which have since been worn down. Because they are so old they have had a long time to be eroded, yet their hard rocks have survived better than the soft rocks in the south-east. Later, during the **Ice Age** (Quaternary period, ending about 10 000 years ago), glaciers covered most of northern Britain and carved the uplands into the dramatic shapes seen today.

bullets: **River Severn**: the longest river in the UK (about 354 km), rises in the Cambrian Mountains (Plynlimon), flows through Shrewsbury, Worcester and Gloucester to the **Bristol Channel**; has the second-highest tidal range in the world and a tidal bore.
**River Thames**: about 346 km, rises in the Cotswolds, flows east through Oxford and London to the **North Sea**; the Thames Barrier protects London from tidal surges.
**River Trent**: flows from Staffordshire to join the Ouse and form the **Humber estuary** (North Sea).

**River Tyne, Tees and Wear** (north-east England), **River Mersey** (north-west, to the Irish Sea), **River Dee and Wye** (Wales and border), **River Clyde, Forth and Tay** (Scotland; the Tay is Scotland's longest river), **River Great Ouse** (East Anglia, to the Wash).
Rivers rising in the Pennines flow east (towards the North Sea) and west (towards the Irish Sea).
**Drainage basin**: the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries; **watershed**: the edge of high land separating basins.
Estuaries (Humber, Thames, Severn, Mersey) are important sites for ports and wetlands.
core.h: Major river systems of the UK
core.p: The UK's rivers are fed by rainfall in the wetter west and flow down from the uplands towards the sea. The high watershed (the **drainage divide**) runs close to the west side of Britain, so the longest rivers generally flow east or south-east to the North Sea, English Channel or Irish Sea. You need to know the names and locations of the major rivers and be able to place them on a map.

bullets: **Hard rock coasts**: Cornwall (granite and slate), north-west Scotland, Pembrokeshire; cliffs, headlands, caves, arches and stacks, slow erosion.
**Soft rock coasts**: Holderness (clay, up to 2 m a year lost, one of Europe's fastest-eroding coasts), Norfolk and Suffolk (soft cliffs), Christchurch Bay.

**Chalk and limestone coasts**: Seven Sisters, Dover (white cliffs), and the **Jurassic Coast** in Dorset and Devon (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) that includes Lulworth Cove, Durdle Door and Old Harry Rocks.
**Depositional coasts**: Spurn Head (spit, Holderness), Chesil Beach (bar, Dorset), Dungeness (shingle foreland), and salt marshes in estuaries.
The **longest fetch** (distance of open water over which wind blows) is to the south-west, so the south and west coasts get the most powerful waves.
Low-lying east and south-east coasts are also at risk from **rising sea level** and storm surges because land there is sinking slowly (isostatic readjustment) as northern Britain rises.
core.h: Coasts of the UK: an overview
core.p: The UK has around 17 000 km of coastline, with a wide variety of features because the coast is made of many different rock types and is exposed to different wave conditions. Hard rocks produce high, rocky coasts (the north and west) while soft rocks produce low coasts that retreat quickly (the south and east). This overview leads directly into the coastal landscapes topic.

bullets: **Geology -> relief**: resistant rocks stand out as hills and mountains; weaker rocks are worn down faster into lowlands and valleys.
**Relief -> climate**: uplands are cooler (temperature drops about 1 degree C per 100 m) and wetter; lowlands in the south-east are warmer and drier, so they are better for crops.
**Climate -> rivers**: high rainfall in the west gives steep, fast-flowing, flashy rivers with high energy in their upper course.
**Rivers -> lowlands**: rivers erode in the uplands and deposit in the lowlands, creating fertile alluvial soils.
**Landscape -> land use**: uplands for sheep farming, forestry, reservoirs, tourism and quarrying; lowlands for arable farming, cities, industry and transport.
Always back up statements with **place names and figures** (heights, lengths, rainfall) to reach the top mark band.
core.h: Explaining the pattern: putting it together
core.p: A strong geography answer links the three ideas: tectonic history and rock type produce the basic relief, ice sculpts the uplands, and rivers and the sea erode and deposit. The relationship is cause and effect: hard rock leads to resistant, high relief; soft rock leads to low relief; high relief in the west leads to heavy rainfall and many rivers; the rivers flow eastwards across the lowlands, where they deposit material and form floodplains and estuaries.

bullets: UK has **15 National Parks** (10 in England, 3 in Wales, 2 in Scotland)—protected areas with special planning controls.
**Reservoirs** (e.g. Kielder Water in Northumberland, Lake Vyrnwy in Wales) store water in the wet uplands for cities in the drier lowlands.
**Tourism** (walking, climbing, sailing) brings income to uplands but can cause footpath erosion, traffic and litter.
**Farming**: hill sheep farming in uplands, arable and horticulture on the fertile lowlands of East Anglia.
**Quarrying** takes limestone, granite, slate and chalk; creates jobs but damages landscapes.
Conflicts of interest arise between residents, farmers, tourists, conservationists and developers; planners must balance them (sustainability).
Link: later topics on rivers and coasts consider management (flood defences, coastal protection).
core.p: People use and change the physical landscape. Upland areas are protected as **National Parks** (e.g. Lake District, Snowdonia, Dartmoor, Peak District) to conserve scenery while allowing recreation and farming. Lowland areas are often built on, drained or farmed intensively. Rivers are dammed for water supply and flood defences, and coasts are protected by hard and soft engineering. Understanding the physical landscape helps decide where and how it can be used sustainably.

bullets: **Describe a distribution**: say where it is (north, west), where it is not, give examples with names, quote figures, and mention anomalies (exceptions).
Use compass directions and phrases such as 'generally', 'mostly concentrated in', 'fewer in'.
On an atlas map, use the **scale** and key; measure distances with a ruler and convert using the scale bar.
On **OS maps**, give grid references: four figures (squares) or six figures (precise); eastings first, then northings ('along the corridor, then up the stairs').
For **spot heights and contours**, state the highest and lowest values and calculate **relief** = highest minus lowest point.
To calculate gradient on a map: **gradient = change in height / horizontal distance** (both in the same units).
Never confuse **describe** (what the pattern is) with **explain** (why it exists).
core.h: Skills: describing distributions and using maps
core.p: This spec point is heavily map-based. Examiners expect you to interpret **relief maps, OS maps, geological maps and river maps**, and to describe patterns using geographical vocabulary. The best descriptions mention **general pattern, direction, place names, figures and anomalies**.

bullets: **Coasts**: rock type and wave energy control which coastal landforms develop.
**Rivers**: relief and rainfall control the long profile of a river and flood risk.
**Glaciation**: explains many upland landforms such as U-shaped valleys and corries.
**Urban issues and the economy**: the largest cities (London, Manchester, Birmingham) are in lowlands with good transport links.
**Climate change**: rising sea level threatens low-lying east-coast areas; wetter winters increase flood risk in river valleys.
**Fieldwork**: both the physical fieldwork (e.g. river or coast) and the human fieldwork use these map skills.
core.h: Link to other topics and wider context
core.p: The overview of the UK's physical landscape is the foundation of Paper 1 'Living with the physical environment'. It connects to the coasts and rivers topics, to glaciation, to the hazards of flooding and erosion, and to human geography topics such as why cities developed where they did, and why agriculture varies. It also illustrates the idea that physical geography and human geography are interdependent.

exam: **Describe** (1 mark per point): give pattern + direction + place name + figure, e.g. 'Highland areas are mainly in the north and west, such as the Scottish Highlands, where Ben Nevis reaches 1345 m.'
**Explain** (2 to 4 marks): use a chain of reasoning with connectives: 'because', 'which leads to', 'therefore'; e.g. hard rock -> resists erosion -> stands out as upland.
For a **4-mark** map description, aim for two developed points (each with a place and figure) plus an anomaly.
Use **geographical vocabulary** (relief, resistant, permeable, watershed, drainage basin); marks are given for correct terminology.
**Locate** on a blank outline map: label with a clear line and neat name; use the atlas map skills you practised.
**Using OS maps**: always give four- or six-figure grid references with eastings first; measure distances with the scale.
**Gradient questions**: gradient = change in height / distance; check both are in metres.
**Compare** questions need both sides: 'In contrast, the south-east is lowland because...'.
Use **'generally'** or **'mostly'** to avoid overgeneralising; mention at least one exception for top marks.
**Command words**: State/Name (1 mark), Describe (what), Explain (why), Assess (weigh up and conclude).

mistakes.r: Only the north and west are highland; the south and east are generally lowland. Use 'generally' and name areas.
Lowland means low in altitude (below about 200 m); it can still be gently rolling, e.g. the Weald.
Ben Nevis (1345 m) in Scotland is the UK's highest; Snowdon (1085 m) is the highest in Wales; Scafell Pike (978 m) the highest in England.
mistakes.w: Ben Nevis is in England / Snowdon is the highest in the UK.

mistakes.r: The Severn (about 354 km) is the longest; the Thames (about 346 km) is the longest entirely in England.
mistakes.w: The Thames is the longest river in the UK.

mistakes.r: Name areas and quote heights from the map; examiners reward specific evidence.
mistakes.w: Describing without place names or figures.

mistakes.r: 'Describe' wants the pattern only; do not waste time on reasons unless asked to explain.
Soft rock erodes quickly and forms low land and bays; hard (resistant) rock forms cliffs and headlands.
mistakes.w: Soft rock is hard-wearing and forms cliffs.

mistakes.r: It is a general guide; there are exceptions, so say 'broadly' or 'generally'.
mistakes.w: The Tees-Exe line is an exact boundary.

summary: This spec point asks for an overview of the UK's physical landscape: where the main upland and lowland areas and river systems are, how rock type and relief explain the north-west highland and south-east lowland pattern, and how to describe it with maps. It matters because every later topic (coasts, rivers, glaciation, hazards) builds on this basic picture.

terms.d: The height and shape of the land surface, including its steepness.
Higher ground, generally above about 200 m, with steeper slopes and often harder rock.
Lower, flatter land, generally below about 200 m, often on softer rocks.
The height of land above sea level, measured in metres.
A line on a map joining places of equal height above sea level.
The study of the rocks that make up an area, their type, structure and age.
Rock formed when molten magma or lava cools and solidifies, e.g. granite and basalt.
Rock formed from layers of sediment compressed and cemented over time, e.g. limestone, chalk, clay.
Rock changed by heat and pressure, e.g. slate and marble.
Rock that is hard and erodes slowly, forming upland, cliffs and headlands.
An imaginary line from the River Tees to the River Exe dividing older, harder rocks (north-west) from younger, softer rocks (south-east).
The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries.
The edge of highland that separates one drainage basin from another.
The tidal mouth of a river where fresh water meets the sea.
Rain caused when moist air is forced to rise over high ground, cools and condenses.
A protected area of countryside with special planning controls to conserve landscape and allow recreation.
Allowing water to pass through, e.g. chalk and limestone.

worked.ans: Upland areas are mainly found in the north and west of the UK (1), for example the Scottish Highlands, the Lake District and Snowdonia (1). The highest is Ben Nevis at 1345 m in the Highlands (1). In contrast, the south and east, such as East Anglia, is generally lowland and flat, although there are lower chalk uplands like the Downs and Chilterns (1). (4 marks)

worked.ans: The south-east is mostly made of younger sedimentary rocks such as clay and chalk (1). These are softer and less resistant, so they have been eroded more easily (1) and have been worn down to low, gentle relief, unlike the harder igneous and metamorphic rocks of the north-west which form upland (1).
